rv.q: For 90 largely plotless minutes, theatergoers are riveted to this play, unable to extricate themselves from both the performances and the show itself.
Molina, an actor in constant demand on both sides of the pond, plays Rothko at full titanic force.
As forcefully delivered in Molina’s volcanic performance, this torrent of observations is consistently engrossing.
The success of Logan’s smart, eloquent entertainment is to bring us in there with him.
What we see, above all, is an artist seeing, and it’s impossible not to feel thrilled by the privilege.
The actor inhabits Rothko completely, giving one of those unnerving performances that makes you believe in the possibility of reincarnation.
Alfred Molina is majestic as Rothko, defying the future he reads in the face of Eddie Redmayne, who holds his own as Rothko’s young assistant.
Love, loyalty, honesty, kindness and status are among the values tested by the hard times that Grimm lays out in this resonant, solidly crafted piece, handsomely mounted by Kate Whoriskey.
This is a booming, blustery Molina (who'll be tough to beat come Tony Awards time) as the man whose genius was perhaps outstripped only by the enormity of his ego.
The most intellectually stimulating 90 minutes Broadway has seen in years.
"Red" is a compelling example of how a thinking theater can simultaneously entertain and educate.
There's barely a cliché left unturned in John Logan's 'Red.'
It turns out to be an engrossing look at Abstract Expressionist painter Mark Rothko.

cn.t: Logan's cerebral two-hander about Mark Rothko draws praise for its intellectual firepower and Molina's commanding performance, though some critics find the script overly reliant on clichés and exclamation-point theatrics.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
